analysis.one_liner: Extends health coverage by banning preexisting-condition denials, creating insurance marketplaces, subsidizing private plans, and expanding Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee reported this health coverage bill on October 19, 2009 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote; the health law Congress ultimately passed in March 2010 grew from this same committee blueprint.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the Senate Finance Committee's health care bill: it would bar insurers from rejecting people with preexisting conditions, require insurers to sell and renew coverage to everyone, set minimum essential benefits with no annual or lifetime limits, and create state marketplaces where people could buy coverage with federal premium credits. It added a Medicaid eligibility category for adults who were previously shut out, taxed people who went without coverage, fined large employers who did not offer insurance, and paid for it partly with annual fees on drug makers, medical device makers, and health insurers. The bill never came to a vote in the Senate, but its framework became the basis of the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans, especially those priced out or rejected because of preexisting conditions; low- and moderate-income families who would receive premium credits and cost-sharing subsidies; previously excluded adults newly eligible for Medicaid; small businesses claiming a new tax credit; and Medicare beneficiaries, who would get a discount on brand-name drugs in the coverage gap and free annual wellness visits.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits health plans in the individual and small group markets from excluding coverage for preexisting conditions or limiting coverage based on health status, and requires guaranteed issue and renewal [S2].

Requires an essential benefits package with little or no cost-sharing and no annual or lifetime limits on coverage, and sets up state exchanges with premium credits and cost-sharing subsidies for people who qualify [S2].
Creates a new mandatory Medicaid eligibility category for all non-elderly, non-pregnant individuals who are otherwise ineligible for Medicaid [S2].
Gives small employers a tax credit for employee health insurance expenses [S2] and establishes a federal program to help start nonprofit, member-run health insurance cooperatives [S3].
Establishes a Medicare prescription drug discount program for brand-name drugs in the coverage gap and adds free annual wellness visits and other preventive coverage [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the credits, subsidies, and Medicaid expansion. People who remain uninsured pay an excise tax. Employers who do not cover full-time workers face penalties. Branded drug manufacturers, medical device makers, and health insurers pay new annual fees, and holders of high-cost employer plans pay an excise tax on the plan's excess value. Limits on flexible spending accounts and health savings accounts also raise revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, the uninsured, large employers, drug and device makers

drawbacks.text: People who choose not to buy coverage would owe a tax penalty (an excise tax on individuals without essential health benefits coverage) [S2].
The bill taxes generous employer health plans through an excise tax on high-cost coverage, a cost that employers and workers with those plans would bear directly [S2].
Employers that fail to meet coverage requirements for full-time employees would pay a penalty, which critics said could discourage hiring [S2].

There is no government-run public plan option; all subsidized coverage runs through private plans, with nonprofit cooperatives offered as the alternative, which keeps private insurers as the permanent channel for the new federal money [S2],[S3].

A fail-safe mechanism requires the President to instruct the HHS and Treasury Secretaries to make reductions in exchange credits and subsidies if the provisions would increase the deficit, meaning the help people receive could be automatically cut [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a large, genuine expansion of coverage: it ends the practice of rejecting sick people, subsidizes premiums for millions, and opens Medicaid to adults who had been excluded. The costs are real but distributed: new taxes on the uninsured, employers, high-cost plans, and three industries, plus federal spending on credits and Medicaid. The main design tradeoff is that the affordability help flows through private insurers, who gain a guaranteed, government-subsidized customer base in exchange for covering the sick — a bargain that delivers coverage but locks insurers into the center of American health care.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was reported by the Finance Committee and placed on the Senate calendar in October 2009, but the Senate never took it up; the majority leader instead advanced a House bill, H.R. 3590, built on the same Finance Committee blueprint, which passed in December 2009 and became the Affordable Care Act in March 2010.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced S. 1796 on October 19, 2009 as an original committee measure [S5].
The committee reported the measure to the Senate with written report 111-89, and additional views and minority views were filed [S5].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 184 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill sat on the calendar and never received a Senate floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

Instead of taking up S. 1796, the Senate used a House bill, H.R. 3590, as the vehicle for its health care legislation; that bill followed the Finance Committee's framework and became the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, signed into law in March 2010.

The bill's substance included insurance market reforms, an essential benefits package, exchanges, premium credits, an individual mandate enforced by an excise tax, employer responsibility requirements, Medicaid expansion, and annual fees on branded pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and health insurance providers [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead in substance: the coverage expansion and consumer protections in this bill became law through the Affordable Care Act. Health insurers and drug makers also came out ahead, because the final law preserved the mandate-and-subsidy architecture that guaranteed them millions of new paying customers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The previously uninsured; insurers and drug makers too

for.name: Max Baucus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as an original committee measure, reported it to the Senate with report 111-89, and placed it on the Senate calendar

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Made overhauling health insurance a top priority and pressed Congress to pass a health care bill through 2009 and 2010

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought S. 1796 to the Senate floor; instead used a House bill, H.R. 3590, as the vehicle for the chamber's health care legislation

against.name: Senate Republican members of the Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views against the bill in the committee's written report; no Republican cosponsored it

against.name: Pharmaceutical and health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Negotiated the fee-and-mandate terms of the Senate Finance framework and publicly backed the committee's approach rather than fighting it

sides.party_line_note: Not a single senator cosponsored the bill and the committee report carried minority views [S4],[S5]; the Senate health law that followed this blueprint ultimately passed with no Republican votes, while Democrats were divided among themselves over details like the public option.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to accept everyone, cover preexisting conditions, and meet benefit and rating rules — but in exchange it makes every American buy their product and routes all federal subsidies through them, making private insurance the permanent channel for publicly funded coverage. They also pay a new annual fee on health insurance providers [S2],[S3].

They pay an annual fee on branded pharmaceuticals and give Medicare beneficiaries a discount in the coverage gap, but they gain millions of newly insured customers whose drug costs are partly paid by federal credits [S2].
The bill imposes an annual fee on medical device manufacturers and importers, a direct cost on the industry [S2].

Employers face a penalty for failing to cover full-time workers and an excise tax on high-cost plans, but employer plans covering retirees receive a temporary federal reinsurance program that reimburses 80% of claims over $15,000 per retiree [S2],[S3].
The bill creates a federal program to help establish nonprofit, member-run health insurance issuers, intended as consumer-owned competition in the exchanges [S2],[S3].
